data.title: How we work with you.
data.photo_alt: A sunlit kitchen counter with a grain bowl, a bottle of olive oil, a lemon half and a pot of basil
data.intro: Coaching here means regular, practical conversations about what you cook, buy and eat. Nothing is complicated, and nothing is on a clock.

children.text: What a session looks like

Sessions run by video call and last 30 to 45 minutes. We start with what happened since last time: what you cooked, what you skipped, what was easy. Then we pick one or two things to try before the next call. You get a short written summary the same day.
What we work on together
Most people come with a few specific questions. These are the topics that come up most often.
Planning a week of meals around your work, family and budget, and writing a shopping list that matches it.
Cooking a few basics well, such as a grain, a tray of roasted vegetables and a sauce, so that meals can be put together quickly.
Making breakfast, lunch and snacks less of a scramble: what to keep in the fridge, what to batch cook on Sunday.
Eating out, travelling and holidays without feeling that the plan has fallen apart.
How we think about food

We look at what you already eat and build from there. We do not ban foods, count points or ask you to weigh anything unless you want to. Recipes on this site are examples of the style: vegetables, grains, beans, some fish and meat, and plenty of flavour.
What coaching is not

We do not diagnose, treat or manage medical conditions, and we do not give advice on medication. If you have a medical condition, an allergy or you are pregnant, speak to your doctor or a registered dietitian first. We are happy to work alongside their advice.
Getting started
Send a request with the Start form. We reply within two working days to arrange a free 20-minute intro call, where you can ask questions before choosing a package.

data.title: A small practice built around home cooking.
data.photo_alt: Hands chopping kale on a wooden board with a chef's knife
data.intro: Everyday Nutrition is a fictional coaching practice used to show this theme. The text below is sample content you can replace.

children.text: The practice

We run coaching calls, publish recipes and keep a small test kitchen where every recipe on the site is cooked before it is written down. There is no shop and no supplement range. The work is conversations, plans and recipes.
Who it is for
People who want to cook more often and eat with less stress: busy parents, people who work from home, students sharing a flat, and anyone whose week has no room for a complicated plan.
What you will not find here

No before and after photos, no promises about weight or health, and no testimonials. This demo business lists no qualifications. If you use the theme for a real practice, add yours, along with any registration your country requires.
Visit or call
Calls happen online. The test kitchen is open for pre-booked sessions on Tuesdays. Contact details and hours are in the footer and on the Start page.

data.format: Four weekly video calls of 45 minutes, a written meal plan template and a shopping list built around the meals you actually like.
data.sessions: One video call a week, message check-in between calls
data.includes:
Free 20-minute intro call
Review of your usual week of food, shopping and cooking
Four 45-minute video calls
A weekly meal plan template you can reuse
A shopping list for the first two weeks
Written summary after every call
Message support on weekdays

children.text: Food Foundations is the usual place to start. In the first call we look at your week as it is: when you shop, who you cook for, what gets eaten on the run. From there we build a plan you can repeat, then adjust it over the next three calls.
A typical month
Week one is the review and a first plan. Week two is shopping and a batch-cooking session. Week three is fixing whatever did not work. Week four is a simple routine you can keep going without us.
Good to know
Everything is run by video call. The meal plan is a template for your own food, not a prescription, and coaching does not replace medical advice.

data.title: Weekly Support
data.summary: Three months of regular calls and messages while new habits settle in.
data.format: A 30-minute call every two weeks and a message check-in each week. We set one small goal per fortnight and review it together.
data.sessions: Video call every two weeks, message check-in every week
data.includes:
Free 20-minute intro call
Six 30-minute video calls
Weekly message check-in
One small goal per fortnight
Recipe suggestions matched to your kitchen and budget
Written summary after every call

children.text: Weekly Support suits people who already know roughly what they want to change and would like someone to check in with. Each fortnight we pick one thing to practise, such as cooking dinner twice more a week or putting together lunches the night before.
How check-ins work
Once a week you send a short message about how things went. We reply within one working day with a note or a question. There is no tracking app and no food diary unless you want one.
Good to know
Prices are sample prices. You can pause for a week if you are away. Coaching does not replace medical advice.

data.format: Three 45-minute video calls with everyone who cooks at home, a shared weekly plan and a bank of recipes that work for adults and children.
data.includes:
Free 20-minute intro call
Three 45-minute video calls
A shared weekly plan for the household
Lunchbox and after-school snack ideas
Ten recipes chosen with your family
A swap list for foods someone dislikes
Message support on weekdays

children.text: Family Table is for households where more than one person cooks, or where meals have to work for people with different tastes. We bring everyone into the calls so that the plan belongs to the whole house.
What we cover
Dinners that can be changed slightly for different people, lunchboxes, weekend batch cooking and what to do when someone refuses what is on the plate.
Good to know
We do not give advice on feeding infants or on medical diets. For those, speak to your doctor or a registered dietitian. Prices are sample prices.

data.title: Roasted sweet potato grain bowl
data.summary: Roasted sweet potato and chickpeas over quinoa with kale, avocado and radish.
data.ingredients:
1 large sweet potato, cut into 2 cm cubes
1 tin chickpeas, drained and dried
1 tablespoon olive oil
1 teaspoon smoked paprika
150 g quinoa
2 handfuls kale, stalks removed
1 avocado, sliced
4 radishes, thinly sliced
2 tablespoons pumpkin seeds
Juice of 1 lemon
Salt and pepper
data.method:
Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the sweet potato and chickpeas with the oil, paprika and a pinch of salt. Roast on a tray for 25 minutes, turning once.
Rinse the quinoa and simmer it in 300 ml water for 12 minutes. Cover and leave for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
Massage the kale with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt for a minute until it softens.
Divide the quinoa between two bowls. Add the kale, sweet potato, chickpeas, avocado and radish.
Finish with pumpkin seeds, the rest of the lemon juice and black pepper.
data.tip: The roasted vegetables and quinoa keep in the fridge for three days. Add the avocado on the day.

data.title: Lentil and roasted vegetable salad
data.summary: Green lentils with roasted courgette and peppers, herbs and a lemon dressing.
data.ingredients:
250 g green or brown lentils
2 courgettes, cut into chunks
2 red peppers, cut into strips
1 red onion, cut into wedges
3 tablespoons olive oil
1 lemon, juice and zest
1 teaspoon Dijon mustard
Small bunch parsley, chopped
Salt and pepper
data.method:
Heat the oven to 210 C. Spread the courgettes, peppers and onion on a tray with 2 tablespoons of the oil and a pinch of salt. Roast for 25 minutes.
Cook the lentils in plenty of simmering water for 20 minutes until tender but not mushy. Drain well.
Whisk the remaining oil with the lemon juice, zest and mustard.
Toss the warm lentils with the dressing, then fold in the vegetables and parsley. Season to taste.
data.tip: Tastes better the next day. Pack it cold for lunch.

data.title: Chicken and kale bowl
data.summary: Sliced chicken thighs with quinoa, kale, red cabbage and roasted sweet potato.
data.ingredients:
3 skinless chicken thighs
1 teaspoon ground cumin
1 tablespoon olive oil
1 small sweet potato, cubed
120 g quinoa
2 handfuls kale
Quarter of a red cabbage, finely shredded
1 avocado
Juice of half a lemon
Salt and pepper
data.method:
Rub the chicken with cumin, salt and half the oil. Leave it for 10 minutes while the oven heats to 220 C.
Roast the sweet potato with the remaining oil for 25 minutes. Add the chicken to the tray after 5 minutes and cook until it is no longer pink inside, about 20 minutes.
Cook the quinoa in 240 ml simmering water for 12 minutes, then rest for 5 minutes.
Steam or blanch the kale for 2 minutes. Slice the chicken.
Assemble the bowls with quinoa, kale, cabbage, sweet potato, chicken and avocado. Squeeze over the lemon.
data.tip: Check the thickest piece of chicken is cooked through before serving.

data.title: Lemon garlic kale
data.summary: A quick side of kale with garlic, olive oil and lemon, ready in the time it takes to rest a roast.
data.ingredients:
250 g curly kale
2 tablespoons olive oil
2 garlic cloves, sliced
Zest and juice of half a lemon
Pinch of chilli flakes
Salt
data.method:
Strip the kale leaves from the stalks and tear them into pieces. Wash and shake dry.
Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the garlic and chilli and cook for 30 seconds without letting the garlic brown.
Add the kale and a splash of water. Stir for 4 to 5 minutes until wilted and bright green.
Take off the heat. Stir in the lemon zest and juice and season with salt.
data.tip: Good under a fried egg for a quick lunch.

data.title: Avocado and tomato toast
data.summary: Toasted sourdough with mashed avocado, tomatoes, seeds and a little lemon.
data.ingredients:
2 thick slices sourdough
1 ripe avocado
1 small handful cherry tomatoes, halved
1 teaspoon lemon juice
1 tablespoon mixed seeds
Olive oil
Salt and pepper
data.method:
Toast the bread until crisp.
Mash the avocado with the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and pepper.
Spread it on the toast. Top with the tomatoes and seeds.
Add a thin drizzle of olive oil.
data.tip: Add a soft-boiled egg if you want something more filling.

data.title: Seeded oat porridge
data.summary: Creamy porridge with toasted pumpkin and sunflower seeds and sliced fruit.
data.ingredients:
100 g rolled oats
400 ml milk or oat drink
1 pinch salt
2 tablespoons pumpkin seeds
1 tablespoon sunflower seeds
1 pear or apple, sliced
1 teaspoon honey or maple syrup
data.method:
Toast the seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes until they pop. Tip them onto a plate.
Put the oats, milk and salt in a pan. Simmer for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until thick.
Spoon into bowls. Top with the fruit, seeds and honey.
data.tip: Make a double batch of toasted seeds and keep them in a jar.

data.title: White bean and basil dip
data.summary: A smooth dip of white beans, basil, lemon and olive oil, good with raw vegetables.
data.ingredients:
1 tin white beans, drained
Large handful fresh basil
1 small garlic clove
3 tablespoons olive oil
Juice of half a lemon
Salt and pepper
Carrot and cucumber sticks, to serve
data.method:
Put the beans, basil, garlic, oil and lemon juice in a food processor.
Blend until smooth, adding a spoonful of water if it is too thick.
Season to taste and chill for 20 minutes before serving with the vegetable sticks.
data.tip: Keeps in the fridge for four days.

data.title: Oat and seed bars
data.summary: Chewy oat bars with seeds and dried fruit, baked in one tin.
data.ingredients:
200 g rolled oats
80 g mixed seeds
80 g dried apricots, chopped
3 ripe bananas, mashed
2 tablespoons peanut butter
1 teaspoon cinnamon
Pinch of salt
data.method:
Heat the oven to 180 C and line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper.
Mix everything in a bowl until it holds together.
Press firmly into the tin and bake for 25 minutes until golden at the edges.
Cool completely in the tin before cutting into 12 bars.
data.tip: Wrap each bar and keep them in the fridge for up to five days.
